clue.text: Fundamental view of language proposed by Ivor Richards

definitions.meaning: fundamental means elementary, at the most simple level

definitions.text: view of language proposed by Ivor Richards
definitions.meaning: I. A. Richards and C. K. Ogden proposed a simplified English of 850 words under this name

explanation.surface: A literary critic puts forward a fundamental theory of language.
explanation.definitionFit: Elementary things are rudimentary, and Ogden and Richards named their pared-down 850-word English after that sense.

clue.text: First beautiful, single joke of Francis

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word beautiful is taken

parts.note: single means one
a crack is a wisecrack or joke

explanation.surface: Someone called Francis tells a first-rate, one-off joke.
explanation.walkthrough: Francis is Dick Francis, the jockey turned thriller writer; the answer is one of his racing novels, so 'of Francis' defines it as a book by him.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1971 racing thriller by the former jockey Dick Francis carries this title.

clue.text: Father with new, attractive singer

parts.note: a sire is a father, especially of an animal

explanation.surface: A dad teams up with a fresh, glamorous vocalist.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth these sea nymphs lured sailors to wreck with their alluring song.

clue.text: Canons applying to most books

definitions.meaning: a cathedral's canons together form its governing body, called by this name
most books are divided into numbered sections of this kind

explanation.surface: Church laws are said to govern most volumes.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral's body of clergy bears this collective name, and the main divisions of a book share it.

clue.text: Lucy, though distracted with cars around, recognizes classic thief

indicators.note: around means the word for cars is placed outside the jumbled letters

parts.note: autos is a word for cars

indicators.note: distracted means confused, so the letters of Lucy are jumbled

explanation.surface: A preoccupied woman among cars spots a famous robber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' and 'recognizes' are link words. Autolycus is the master thief of Greek myth and the rogue pedlar in Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend the son of Hermes was a cunning stealer of cattle, and Shakespeare borrowed the name for a pickpocket.

clue.text: Silver is needed for Spartan king

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A Spartan monarch needs silver.
explanation.definitionFit: Several kings of ancient Sparta bore this name, notably the reformer of the third century BC.

clue.text: Haydn tests composition — a dramatic epic

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so the letters of Haydn tests are rearranged

explanation.surface: A composer's work is tested, producing a grand drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composition' looks musical beside Haydn, but it signals the anagram. The answer is Thomas Hardy's epic drama of the Napoleonic wars.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's long verse drama about the Napoleonic wars bears this title.

clue.text: Small case for Gay's warder, say

indicators.note: say signals that the warder's name is spoken and sounds like the answer

parts.note: Lockit is the jailer in John Gay's The Beggar's Opera

explanation.surface: A small container is needed by a playwright's prison guard.
explanation.walkthrough: Lockit, keeper of Newgate gaol in John Gay's The Beggar's Opera, sounds like a small hinged case.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny hinged pendant case worn on a chain holds a portrait or a lock of hair.

clue.text: Did Chrétien imply Lancelot was one such, left in the cart?

definitions.text: Did Chrétien imply Lancelot was one such, left in the cart?

parts.words: Did Chrétien imply Lancelot was one such, left in the cart?
parts.note: Chrétien de Troyes wrote a romance whose French title calls Lancelot the knight of the cart

explanation.surface: A question about whether a medieval poet implied his hero was abandoned in a wagon.
explanation.walkthrough: Chrétien de Troyes titled his Lancelot romance Le Chevalier de la Charrette, the Knight of the Cart: Lancelot rides in a cart in it.
explanation.definitionFit: French for a knight or horseman, it is the word Chrétien used in his title for Lancelot.

clue.text: Dramatist heard to carol often at the Abbey

indicators.note: heard means the word for carol is spoken and matches the answer's sound

parts.note: to carol is to sing

explanation.surface: A playwright is heard singing carols regularly at the Abbey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'often at the Abbey' points to the Abbey Theatre in Dublin, where J. M. Synge's plays were staged.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Synge was the Irish playwright of The Playboy of the Western World.

clue.text: Story somehow pieced together from tavern air

indicators.note: the letters of tavern air are assembled in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A tale is cobbled together from pub atmosphere.
explanation.definitionFit: An account of connected events is a tale or story.

clue.text: Athenian demagogue reveals swindle about the French

indicators.note: about means the swindle word goes round the French article

parts.note: a con is a swindle
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A rabble-rouser from Athens exposes a fraud involving the French.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleon was the populist Athenian leader in the Peloponnesian War, mocked by Aristophanes.

clue.text: Danish king is able to join pick-up vehicle

parts.note: can means is able
a ute, short for utility vehicle, is a pick-up truck in Australian usage

explanation.surface: A Danish monarch is able to climb into a truck.
explanation.definitionFit: Cnut, the eleventh-century Danish ruler of England, is famous for the tale of commanding the tide.

clue.text: Gothic, perhaps — or Roman, even

parts.note: Gothic and Roman read like architecture or history but are styles of printed lettering

explanation.surface: A remark about architectural or historical styles.
explanation.walkthrough: Gothic (blackletter) and roman are both styles of print, so each is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A design of printed letters, such as roman or blackletter, is a font style.

clue.text: Hardy heroine is non-committal

definitions.meaning: Paula Power, heroine of a Thomas Hardy novel, is the lukewarm figure of its title
Laodicea's church was rebuked in Revelation for being lukewarm, hence one indifferent in belief

explanation.surface: A Thomas Hardy heroine refuses to commit herself.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's 1881 novel is named for its indifferent heroine, after the lukewarm church of Revelation.

clue.text: Member of George Johnston's test team?

definitions.text: Member of George Johnston's test team?

parts.words: Member of George Johnston's test team?
parts.note: George Johnston was a writer from Melbourne, so his national cricket side is the one meant

explanation.surface: A question about a player in a writer's cricket side.
explanation.walkthrough: George Johnston wrote My Brother Jack; a Test team is a national cricket side, so his would be his country's.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from Johnston's homeland would play for that country's national cricket side.

clue.text: Italian film outlines

parts.note: the word for a film's plot outline is borrowed from Italian

explanation.surface: Sketches of films from Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Screenplay outlines take a name borrowed from Italian theatre, where it meant the plot sketch.

clue.text: Greene's fruity Harry in the bronze medal position

definitions.text: Greene's fruity Harry in the bronze medal position

parts.words: Greene's fruity Harry in the bronze medal position
parts.note: Graham Greene's Harry in The Third Man shares his surname with a citrus fruit, and third place takes bronze

explanation.surface: A novelist's character finishes third.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Lime is the villain of Graham Greene's The Third Man; third man is the bronze medallist.
explanation.definitionFit: The citrus fruit gives its name to the racketeer at the heart of The Third Man.

clue.text: Writers like Hazlitt first in attempts

indicators.note: in places the first word inside the word for attempts

parts.note: essays are attempts
1st, written with I for 1, gives IST

explanation.surface: Writers such as Hazlitt come first in tries.
explanation.walkthrough: First written as the ordinal 1st, with the figure 1 read as the letter I, is a common crossword device.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hazlitt was a master of the short prose piece, like Lamb and Montaigne.

clue.text: Queen with attendant at Windsor

parts.note: Anne was Queen of Great Britain from 1702 to 1714
a page is a young attendant

explanation.surface: A queen and her servant at Windsor Castle.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a character found 'at Windsor': Anne Page is the young woman courted in Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's comedy The Merry Wives of Windsor has her as Master Page's daughter, wooed by three suitors.

clue.text: Uneven keel makes for blue horseman

indicators.note: uneven suggests the letters of keel are put out of order

explanation.surface: A lopsided boat keel serves a sad rider.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Klee belonged to Der Blaue Reiter, the Blue Rider group of painters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swiss painter Paul Klee was associated with Der Blaue Reiter, the Munich artists' group.

clue.text: King of Norway might be a first-born

indicators.note: might be suggests the letters of a first-born could be reshuffled into the answer

explanation.surface: A Norwegian king could be an eldest child.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the Norwegian prince in Hamlet who takes the Danish throne at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hamlet the young Norwegian prince arrives at the close to claim the Danish crown.

clue.text: Imitation was intrinsic to his oeuvre

definitions.text: Imitation was intrinsic to his oeuvre

parts.words: Imitation was intrinsic to his oeuvre
parts.note: the American poet's 1961 book of loose translations was titled Imitations

explanation.surface: A remark that a writer's work depended on copying.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Lowell's Imitations (1961) is a collection of free versions of European poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Lowell published a celebrated book of loose verse translations called Imitations.

clue.text: Philosopher's view of strange mountain pick-me-up

indicators.note: strange means the letters of the mountain word are made odd, rearranged

parts.note: an alp is a mountain
a tonic is a pick-me-up

explanation.surface: A thinker considers an odd peak a restorative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'view of' is a link to the definition; Platonic means of or after Plato, the philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to Plato, the Athenian thinker, is the sense of this adjective.

clue.text: High point, so to speak, reached by fantasist

indicators.note: so to speak signals that the word for high point is spoken and gives the name

parts.note: a peak is a high point

explanation.surface: A summit, as it were, is reached by a dreamer.
explanation.walkthrough: Mervyn Peake wrote the Gormenghast fantasy novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Mervyn Peake created the gothic fantasy world of Gormenghast.

clue.text: He calmly gave his address to some people in America

definitions.text: He calmly gave his address to some people in America

parts.words: He calmly gave his address to some people in America
parts.note: the founder of Methodism preached in Georgia and was famous for preaching calmly to hostile crowds

explanation.surface: A man serenely delivers a speech to Americans.
explanation.walkthrough: John Wesley, founder of Methodism, preached in Georgia in the 1730s; his address can also be his sermon.
explanation.definitionFit: John Wesley, the Methodist founder, went as a missionary to the colony of Georgia.

clue.text: Defamation in glib, elegant writing

indicators.note: in shows the answer lies within the words glib and elegant

explanation.surface: Slick, polished prose can be slanderous.
explanation.definitionFit: Damaging falsehood published in writing is a legal wrong of this name.

clue.text: Dream of barrister to become part-time bestselling writer

definitions.meaning: a dream is a wish or aspiration

definitions.text: barrister to become part-time bestselling writer
definitions.meaning: Anthony Hawkins, a barrister, wrote The Prisoner of Zenda under a pen name

explanation.surface: A lawyer dreams of becoming a best-selling author in spare time.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Hope (Hawkins) practised at the bar while writing The Prisoner of Zenda.
explanation.definitionFit: A dream is an aspiration, and Anthony Hawkins wrote his bestselling Zenda novel under this pen name while a barrister.

clue.text: She jumps from the pages of Shute's work

definitions.text: She jumps from the pages of Shute's work

parts.words: She jumps from the pages of Shute's work
parts.note: Nevil Shute's novel A Town Like ... ends its title with a girl's name

explanation.surface: A female character leaps out of a novelist's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Nevil Shute's novel A Town Like Alice puts the name on its cover.
explanation.definitionFit: Nevil Shute's novel is named after Alice Springs, the outback town in central Australia.

clue.text: Turncoat Roman strategist could have been Nero's babu

indicators.note: could have been suggests the letters of Nero's babu might be rearranged into a different name

explanation.surface: A traitorous Roman general might have been the emperor's clerk.
explanation.walkthrough: Enobarbus deserts Antony for Octavius in Antony and Cleopatra. A babu is an Indian clerk.
explanation.definitionFit: In Antony and Cleopatra, Antony's lieutenant abandons him for Octavius and then dies of remorse.

clue.text: Point taken by girl in Victorian novel

parts.note: east is a point of the compass
Lynne is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl gets the point in a nineteenth-century book.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Henry Wood's 1861 sensation novel was one of the great Victorian bestsellers.

clue.text: Not The Bell, but one of three ()

definitions.text: Not The Bell, but one of three ()

parts.words: Not The Bell, but one of three ()
parts.note: the Brontë sisters published as three Bells, Currer, Acton and this one

explanation.surface: A puzzle about a bell and a trio.
explanation.walkthrough: Emily Brontë wrote as Ellis Bell; the clue wants the first name, not the surname Bell.
explanation.definitionFit: Emily Brontë's pen name was this forename with the surname Bell.
